messages.subject: Promoter array, UGP, etc.
parts:
Hi Henrik (mostly).

(Thought I'd include the whole list in case others want to contribute
or suggest what I'm thinking of doing is futile ...)

What I am planning on doing is improving (creating?) support within
aroma.affymetrix for tiling arrays. Specifically the Human Promoter
Tiling array 1.0R, but most of this will generalize to the others. So
far, I've been making bare-bones CDF files direct from the bpmap files
(unit=chromosome). I'm almost finished making a CDF that is promoter-
centric (unit=promoter), given the annotation from Affymetrix (which
I've just learned is somewhat incomplete).

One question. You have UGP (UnitGroupPosition) files - AromaUgpFile
objects. For you, each unit is (usually) a SNP and therefore would
have one genomic location. For me, each unit is a promoter and then
each probe within a promoter has its own position, typically non-
regular spacing as well. I'll probably also need to store strand and
location of the TSS for each unit.

Is there an easy way to store this info in the AromaUgpFiles? Or, a
simple extension of it?

In the future, I'd like to recreate MAT (model-based analysis of
tiling arrays -- Shirley Liu's) with the possibility of including
extra terms in the model, or at least having an R version of it.
Henrik has already built in functionality for some of this.

Mark

> (unit=chromosome). I'm almost finished making a CDF that is promoter-
> centric (unit=promoter), given the annotation from Affymetrix (which
> I've just learned is somewhat incomplete).

This is great and I think it is possible too - we might have to
fine/adjust aroma.affymetrix slightly, but lets see.

>
> One question. You have UGP (UnitGroupPosition) files - AromaUgpFile
> objects. For you, each unit is (usually) a SNP and therefore would
> have one genomic location. For me, each unit is a promoter and then
> each probe within a promoter has its own position, typically non-
> regular spacing as well. I'll probably also need to store strand and
> location of the TSS for each unit.

You probably meant to write this, but the UGP is actually for Unit
*Genome* Position and maps (unit, chromosome, position), where the
'unit' [index] is implicit by the order. For other who are
interested, more info at:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/unit-genome-position-ugp-files

Yes, the UGP annotation data is unit centric and units are defined by
the CDF. The class that handles UGP maps/files is the AromaUgpFile
class. For more general unit-based mappings, i.e. (unit, <data>,
<data2>, ...), there is the AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile. The
AromaUgpFile is actually a special case of this class. For info of
the former, see also:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/creating-aromaunittabularfile-from-scratch

In turn the superclass of AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile is
AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile, cf:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/aromatabularbinaryfile

Think of it as a binary tab delimited file where each column holds a
predefined data type of certain size (string are not supported).


Another natural way of indexing annotation data according to the CDF
is by not only units but also groups, e.g. here (unit, group,
chromosome, position). There is no class available for this mapping.


Leaving the constraints of the CDF we can also index by probes/cells,
e.g. here (cell, chromosome, position). Such annotation data is
independent of the CDF and if you change the CDF you can still use the
same map because there is a mapping from the CDF to the cells. As you
found out, there is indeed a class for this, namely
AromaCellTabularBinaryFile. Analogously to how
AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile index data by units, this new class index
data by cell indices. Likewise, you can define you own set of columns
(data type and size). For (cell, chromosome, position), you need to
create a AromaCgpFile class which replicated AromaUgpFile but for
cells. You already learned about the AromaCellSequenceFile, and if
you look at the code it is actually inheriting from
AromaCellTabularBinaryFile, because the latter has some general
methods that can be useful.

> Is there an easy way to store this info in the AromaUgpFiles? Or, a
> simple extension of it?

So, you need to create a AromaCgpFile class for this.

...to next message.

/Henrik

On Thu, Oct 23, 2008 at 6:25 PM, Mark Robinson <mrob...@wehi.edu.au> wrote:

> AromaCellSequenceFile object is the ticket to store the sequences for
> each cell.

Yes, it stores the sequences in raw columns, such that the 1st
nucleotide of each probe sequence is in the 1st column, the 2nd
nucleotide in the 2nd column and so on until the 25th probe position.
The nucleotide is encoded as a raw/single byte. Storing it column by
column makes it faster to grab for instance the middle base of all
probes, or say the middle 3 bases. The 26th column hold information
on target strand. AromaCellSequenceFile inherit from
AromaCellTabularBinaryFile, so we can reuse a lot.

>
> AromaCellTabularBinaryFile will allow me to store one other thing for
> every cell (e.g. match scores -- the number of hits to the genome, etc).

>
> The genomic positions is the tricky bit, because some probes map to
> multiple locations. As you mentioned previously, I could associate
> multiple TabularBinaryFiles and for the probes (cells) that map to
> multiple locations populate it.

I recall our chat about this.

CASE 1: SMALL UPPER BOUND OF NUMBER OF POSITIONS PER CELL
If there there is no probe with more than K mappings and K is small,
then I would just allocate the 2*K columns needed and store NAs where
there are no mappings. Example map:

(cell, chromosome[1], position[1], ..., , chromosome[K], position[K])


CASE 2: SMALL UPPER BOUND OF NUMBER OF POSITIONS PER CELL
In case K is too large, I would find the most common number of
mappings, say K*, and use CASE 1 to store the K* first mappings. You
might want to add a column specifying the nbrOfLoci for each cell:

(cell, nbrOfLoci, chromosome[1], position[1], ..., , chromosome[K*],
position[K*])

and then deal with the exceptions separately. This way you will have
quickly access/indexing in most of the cases, i.e. when nbrOfLoci <=
K*. For the cells where nbrOfLoci > K*, you need to figure out how to
store that data in the same file. It is possible, but it is not clear
how to do it. In one way or the other, you need to allocate space
(think memory) for this extra data and you need to be able to find it.
Basically, you need to encode some kind of ragged list structure.
You can allocate extra space by adding auxiliary columns. You have to
create your own mapping and encoding for what you want though. Then
your API is the one that will hide all the details. Another
alternatives is to store the extra mappings in new rows, but you have
to come up with a way to index these rows. Same problem to solve.
(Avoid using the file footer to store this kind of data).

The performance will depend on how ragged or how rectangular your map is.

You'll also have to think how you should return data. You might want
to return data as a list structure, where each element correspond to a
cell and holds a vector of positions.

To make sure I understand you correct: In your CDF, the same cell
index can show up in multiple units, correct?

The closest to this idea is how we read data from CEL files in the
shape of the CDF. This is done by the affxparser package. However,
if the same cell index occur in several units, all you'll get is the
same probe intensity read in all places. It is not possible to read
different values.

So, there is no such CDF-like structure in aroma.affymetrix, except
the CDF/AffymetrixCdfFile itself. You could of course create a CDF
file that holds the data you wish to store (you can even encode other
data types in the existing CDF ones as long as it fits). The you
could create a subclass to AffymetrixCdfFile that hides all the
details.

Before deciding on a file format, maybe it is easier to just "dump"
(using saveObject()) a precreated list structure like the one you show
above and then setup up a class that hides all the details.
Internally it can use loadObject() to read the structure back ones.
Special readUnits() functions will then emulate the access similar to
how it is done for CDFs. This will allow you to procrastinate your
decision on the file format you need to use.

/Henrik

I was suggesting that you keep you current CDF as is, and have another
that carries the genomic locations. For instance, you can encode the
'chromosome' location in 'pbase', and 'position' in 'atom'. If 'atom'
only holds a short (2 bytes), you'll need to encode it in 'indexpos'
as well. This file will formally not be a CDF but you can probably
use the Fusion SDK to read it. I would also have a different file
name ending for it. It is also important that it is clear to what
CDF this "parallel CDF" maps to.

My feeling is that it is better to avoid using the CDF file format for
this, because it is likely to cause problems one day or the other for
either you or the end user. I can see how the wrong "parallel CDF" is
used for a different CDF and so on. Your encoding (pbase, atom &
indexpos) -> (chromosome, position) has to be done each time you read
and probably at the R level, which means that it will be rather slow
(this type of encoding is done when we save PLM fits, and we know it
takes time).

A mapping independent of your CDF is:

(cell, chromsome1, position1, chromsome2, position2, ..., chromsomeK,
positionK) (**)

where K varies with cell. This is basically a ragged list. To speed
things up you can collect you cells into block of equal K size, such
that each block becomes a rectangular matrix. In your case you will
have blocks of 10 different sizes. Each block can be an element in a
list. To access the above mapping (**) given a cell index, you will
have to have a mapping/hash that first brings you to the right block,
and then to the right row of that block.

Yet again, I think it will be useful to first do this in R without
worrying about the file format; use save-/loadObject() to hide that
from the user.
